guides.title: Australopithecus: Every Published Fossil Locality Across Africa
guides.description: Complete species-by-species and basin-by-basin catalogue of 39 published Australopithecus fossil localities across East, Central (Chad), and Southern Africa (~5.0–1.98 Ma).
guides.intro: Between roughly 4.3 million and 1.98 million years ago, hominins of the genus Australopithecus radiated across eastern, central, and southern Africa. Here every published fossil-bearing formation, footprint bed, and cave chamber is catalogued with specimen numbers, radiometric/cosmogenic dating methods, and active taxonomic and chronological debates.
guides.scope: All 39 mapped Australopithecus localities and stratigraphic horizons across Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Chad, and South Africa (~5.0–1.98 Ma).

map.scope: Continental African distribution linking Bahr el Ghazal (Chad), the Afar and Turkana rifts, high Rift shoulders near Nairobi, Laetoli, Makapansgat, Sterkfontein/Malapa, and Taung.

points.label: Koro Toro KT 12/13/40, Chad

points.description: Type site of A. anamensis (Kanapoi), earlier Lothagam mandible, and Lomekwi Kenyanthropus platyops.

paragraphs.text: Fragmentary cf. anamensis jaws at Lothagam (~5.0–4.2 Ma) and Tabarin (~4.45 Ma) precede the first rich radiation of Australopithecus anamensis across the East African Rift between ~4.3 Ma (Ileret mandible, Lewis et al. 2024) and ~3.8 Ma (Woranso-Mille MRD cranium). Along the Awash and Turkana rivers—at Kanapoi (type site, 4.17–4.07 Ma), Asa Issie (4.2–4.1 Ma directly above Ardipithecus ramidus), Fejej, Galili, and Allia Bay—thickened molar enamel and human-like hindlimb tibiae confirm habitual bipedalism in woodland-bushland corridors.

sections.heading: Mid-Pliocene Radiation: A. afarensis, A. deyiremeda, A. bahrelghazali & Late Survivors (3.85–2.5 Ma)

paragraphs.text: Australopithecus afarensis endured for nearly a million years from Belohdelie (~3.89 Ma) and Laetoli (3.85–3.46 Ma) through Woranso-Mille KSD-VP-1/1 ('Kadanuumuu'), Maka (3.4 Ma), Dikika ('Selam'), Hadar (AL 129, Lucy AL 288-1, AL 333 'First Family'), Omo Usno/Shungura, Koobi Fora Tulu Bor, Chemeron, and Kantis near Nairobi (~1,740 m upland Rift shoulder). Yet Woranso-Mille proves mid-Pliocene diversity: between 3.5 and 3.3 Ma, A. afarensis lived side-by-side with A. deyiremeda, whose climbing-adapted Burtele foot was firmly attributed in 2025.

Far west in Chad, the Koro Toro sites (KT 12 'Abel', KT 13, KT 40; ~3.58 Ma) reveal an australopith population (A. bahrelghazali) flourishing along Lake Chad woodland-sedgelands 2,500 km from the Rift. Later still, after 2.8 Ma, Bouri yields megadont A. garhi (~2.5 Ma) while Villmoare et al. (2025) documented a late non-afarensis Australopithecus overlapping chronologically with earliest Homo at Ledi-Geraru (~2.78–2.59 Ma).

sections.heading: Southern African Karst Caves & Dating Controversies (3.76–1.98 Ma)

paragraphs.text: Southern Africa's Australopithecus fossils accumulated inside dolomitic limestone sinkholes at Taung, Makapansgat, Sterkfontein (Jacovec Cavern, Member 2 Silberberg 'Little Foot', Member 4 Sts 5 'Mrs. Ples', Member 5), Gladysvale, and Malapa (1.977 Ma A. sediba). Because caves lack volcanic tuffs, chronology hinges on uranium-lead flowstone dating, mammalian biochronology (~3.0–2.0 Ma for Taung/Makapansgat/Member 4), and 26Al/10Be cosmogenic nuclide burial ages pushing Member 2 'Little Foot' (~3.67 Ma), Jacovec (~3.76 Ma), and Member 4 (~3.4 Ma) back to the Mid-Pliocene.

Alongside age disputes, Ronald Clarke and colleagues distinguish two southern species—A. prometheus (StW 573 'Little Foot' and Makapansgat) and A. africanus—whereas Beaudet (2023) and others interpret the Sterkfontein variation as a single variable species. Newly verified 2025 enamel palaeoproteomic peptides from Member 4 open new biomolecular windows into South African australopiths.

guides.title: Before 1 Million Years Ago: Every Global Hominin & Tool Site (7.0–1.0 Ma)
guides.description: Exhaustive planetary inventory of 164 hominin fossil and archaeological localities dated older than 1.0 Ma across Africa, the Levant, Caucasus, Europe, Asia, and oceanic Wallacea—plus species attributions and dispersal routes.
guides.intro: Every securely dated—and every seriously debated—hominin fossil and Early Stone Age / Mode 1 / Early Acheulean locality on Earth older than 1.0 million years is concentrated exclusively across Africa and parts of Eurasia and Wallacea. None exist in the Americas, Australia/New Guinea, Polynesia, or high Arctic latitudes. This guide documents every known >1 Ma locality globally, the species tied to it, and how hominins reached each frontier.
guides.scope: All 164 published pre-1.0 Ma fossil and archaeological localities across Africa, SW Asia, Caucasus/Anatolia, Europe, India/Pakistan, China, Java, Flores, and Sulawesi (~7.0–1.0 Ma).

sections.heading: African Deep Roots: Hominins, Earliest Tools & Trans-Saharan Spread (7.0–1.0 Ma)

paragraphs.text: All firmly established hominin evolutionary origins prior to ~2.5 million years ago took place inside Africa: Sahelanthropus tchadensis (~7 Ma, Chad), Orrorin tugenensis (~6 Ma, Kenya), Ardipithecus kadabba and ramidus (5.8–4.3 Ma, Ethiopia), Australopithecus (~4.3–1.98 Ma across Chad, East Africa, and South Africa), Kenyanthropus platyops (~3.5 Ma), and Paranthropus (~2.9–1.0 Ma). Stone-tool behavior emerged by ~3.3 Ma at Lomekwi 3 (unknown Pliocene maker, possibly Kenyanthropus or A. afarensis), followed by ~3.0–2.6 Ma early Oldowan flake-and-core assemblages at Nyayanga (with Paranthropus!), Namorotukunan, Ledi-Geraru Bokol Dora, East Gona, and Omo Member F.

By ~2.44 Ma, hominin toolmakers had already crossed a humid 'Green Sahara' corridor to reach Mediterranean Algeria at Aïn Boucherit (Sahnouni et al. 2018), while by 1.76–1.3 Ma early Homo erectus carried Large Cutting Tools (Early Acheulean handaxes and cleavers) from Kokiselei 4, Olduvai FLK West, and Konso to high 2,000–2,400 m Ethiopian plateaus (Melka Kunture & Gadeb), South Africa's Rietputs 15 Vaal gravels (~1.55 Ma), and Thomas Quarry I in Morocco (~1.3 Ma).

sections.heading: Out of Africa I & How Hominins Reached Eurasia & Wallacea (2.5–1.0 Ma)

paragraphs.text: Four primary physical pathways and mechanisms explain how >1 Ma hominins colonized Eurasia and Island Southeast Asia: (1) The Sinai–Jordan Rift corridor: savanna and lake chains during wet Pliocene/Early Pleistocene intervals led early Homo north through Zarqa Valley (~2.48–1.95 Ma), Erq el-Ahmar (~1.9 Ma), and later large-bodied H. erectus at ʿUbeidiya (~1.5 Ma). (2) A possible southern Red Sea (Bab el-Mandeb) or northern Green Arabia littoral pathway connecting Danakil (Buia/Engel Ela) to Nefud paleolakes and the Zarqa/Siwalik piedmont. (3) Across Anatolia, Caucasus, and Eastern European riverplains into Europe—demonstrated at Dmanisi (~1.77 Ma), Grăunceanu (~1.95 Ma cutmarks, Curran et al. 2025), Kocabaş (~1.6–1.2 Ma), Kozarnika (1.6–1.4 Ma), Korolevo I (1.42 Ma), Pirro Nord, Lézignan, Orce, Sima del Elefante ATE7-1 ('Pink', 1.4–1.1 Ma), Vallonnet (1.2 Ma), and Pont-de-Lavaud (1.1 Ma)—whereas no geological/fossil proof supports a Gibraltar Strait ocean crossing at 1.4 Ma.

(4) Across the Asian steppe–loess belt and Indian piedmont into China (Shangchen 2.12 Ma, Xihoudu 2.43/1.27 Ma, Gongwangling 1.63 Ma, Yunxian 1.77 Ma, Yuanmou 1.7 Ma, Nihewan 1.66–1.1 Ma), then south across the exposed Sunda Shelf landbridge into Java (~1.5–1.3 Ma Sangiran/Mojokerto) during glacial sea-level drops. Crucially, Calio on Sulawesi (>1.04 Ma, Hakim et al. 2025 Nature) and Wolo Sege on Flores (1.02 Ma) lie beyond deep ocean straits (Wallace's Line) that never dried out; small founding hominin groups likely crossed these straits via accidental storm-surge or tsunami vegetation rafting.

Transparent boundaries on contested claims & empty continents: Several claimed pre-2 Ma Eurasian/Crete traces—including Crete Trachilos prints (~5.7 Ma), NW India Masol (~2.6 Ma), Germany Untermaßfeld (~1.05 Ma), Taman Kermek/Dagestan Muhkai, and China Renzidong/Longgupo mandible affinities—are plotted explicitly with clear cautions because geofact fracture kinematics, stratigraphic reworking, or non-hominin anatomy remain unresolved. Conversely, Zero confirmed >1 Ma hominin sites exist in the Americas, Sahul/Australia, Pacific islands, Greenland, or high Arctic tundra, which were not reached until Homo sapiens (or Denisovan/Siberian ancestors in northeast Eurasia) much later.
